body.x: A Shia nikah is not complicated, but it is precise: a small number of requirements make the contract valid, and missing one can leave a family unsure whether a marriage actually took place. This checklist sets out what must be in place, why each item matters, and — just as honestly — where Shia scholars differ, so you know which questions belong to your own marja rather than to a website.
The people: consent, wali and witnesses

Start with the people, because every later step depends on them. Both the bride and the groom must consent to the marriage themselves, freely and without coercion; a contract spoken over an unwilling party is not a marriage. For the bride, her wali — her father, or her paternal grandfather — has a formal role: the majority of contemporary marjas hold that a woman marrying for the first time requires her wali's permission for the nikah to be valid, while a woman who has been married before acts for herself. There are differences of detail between marjas, including how the rule applies in particular circumstances, and this is the single most common point on which families write to a marja's office. Witnesses complete the picture: two upright Muslim men witnessing the contract is the near-universal practice and is strongly recommended in Shia law, while jurists discuss whether witnesses are a strict condition of validity for a permanent marriage. No family should treat their presence as optional decoration.

Free consent of bride and groom — both parties agree personally and without pressure; silence under pressure is not consent.
The wali's permission where required — for a first marriage, the agreement of the father or paternal grandfather, in line with your marja's ruling.
Two witnesses present — upright witnesses who hear the offer and acceptance and can attest to the contract afterwards.
Mahr agreed and specified — the amount or nature of the mahr settled before the ceremony, including how much is prompt and how much deferred.
The sigha recited correctly — the offer and acceptance spoken in Arabic, in the past tense, in one sitting, by the couple themselves or by their appointed representatives.
Both parties identified unambiguously — the wording names the specific bride and groom; a contract pronounced over a mistaken identity is no contract.
No legal impediment — neither party is within a waiting period (iddah) from a previous marriage, nor related to the other within the prohibited degrees, nor otherwise barred from marrying.
Representatives properly appointed — if wakils recite the formula, each has actually been authorised by the party they speak for.
The contract documented — the written record signed by the couple, the representatives, the witnesses and the officiant, and kept safely.
The wording itself, and why precision matters

Of all the items on the list, the sigha is the one families most often underestimate. The offer and acceptance are not a blessing said over the couple; they are the marriage. That is why the formula is recited in Arabic — the language in which its legal meaning has been fixed and discussed for centuries — and why it must be in the past tense, completed rather than promised, and why offer and acceptance belong in a single sitting with no gap between them. A couple may recite the words themselves, and some do, but most appoint representatives and let an experienced reciter guide the exact wording, precisely so that nothing turns on a mispronounced name or a half-remembered phrase. Where a party genuinely cannot pronounce the Arabic, scholars discuss what is permitted — another question for your marja, and one to settle before the day, not during it.

Three practical points catch families out. First, the waiting period: a woman whose previous marriage has ended, by divorce or by widowhood, must complete her iddah before a new contract, and the dates should be checked rather than assumed. Second, the mahr is the bride's property outright; arrangements that quietly route it elsewhere, or pressure on the day to forgive it, undermine one of the contract's own protections. Third, civil status: a religiously valid contract may still leave a couple unmarried in the eyes of their country, so civil registration should be planned alongside the aqd, not discovered afterwards.
Where the answer depends on your marja

A checklist can state the mainstream, but Shia practice is lived through taqlid — following a qualified scholar — and honest guidance has to mark its own edges. The wali's permission, the status of witnesses, the exact wording where a party cannot pronounce the Arabic, and unusual cases — an absent wali, a convert without a Muslim guardian, a marriage across legal jurisdictions — are all areas where rulings differ in detail between marjas. None of this is a defect in the process; it is how the tradition is designed to work. Take your specific facts to your marja's office or a scholar you trust, and take them early: every one of these questions is easy before the day and awkward after it.

Work through the list and a Shia nikah reduces to its essentials: two people consenting, a guardian's blessing where required, witnesses listening, a gift agreed, and the words spoken properly. If you are still at the stage before all this — finding the person — Shia Rishta supports the search itself: free profiles, email verification, photos kept private until you share them, wali and guardian involvement, and conversations that begin only when interest is mutual.
